antipatterns: app/Models/Export.php:20 olderThan scope takes int $days and calls now() inside the scope. That ties the scope to the CLI's unit and recomputes the cutoff separately for the dry run and the purge. Passing a Carbon cutoff would be cleaner.
tests/Feature/PurgeExportsTest.php:28-31 the docblock on the test helper explains framework internals and reasoning, which the comments rule says belongs in the PR description
tests/Feature/PurgeExportsTest.php:174,191 uses an inline \Mockery FQCN instead of an import

Tests miss two cases: a purge larger than one lazyById chunk (1000 rows), and a disk delete() that throws rather than returning false. The command handles the throw at PurgeExports.php:77, but no test exercises it.
Invalid --days is only tested with 'abc' and '0'; negative and decimal values are not covered.
strengths: The same solid core design as impl-2. lazyById keeps memory flat and moves forward by id, so rows kept after a failed delete don't stall later chunks; I probed 2500 rows with mixed failures. A Throwable from the disk is reported and treated as a failure, the row is only deleted once its file is gone, and the exit code is FAILURE when any file fails.
ConfirmableTrait with --force; when the operator refuses, the command returns FAILURE; the dry run comes before the confirmation and the lock

Cache::lock with a 6h TTL is more realistic for millions of rows plus file I/O than a 1h TTL. The schedule uses onOneServer, and the command-level lock alone keeps a manual run and the nightly run from overlapping, so the schedule has no redundant withoutOverlapping.
filter_var with min_range validates --days in a single step
Adds the inverse User::exports() HasMany relation
Mocks the real FilesystemAdapter and delegates to the faked disk for the paths that should succeed, which is realistic
The helper is honestly named registerAlwaysConfirmingCommand, and the real production paths (--no-interaction refusal, --force) use detectEnvironment

antipatterns: app/Console/Commands/PurgeExports.php:21 LOCK_SECONDS = 3600. Purging a few million rows, each with its own file delete, can easily run past 1h. The lock would then expire mid-run and a manual run could overlap; withoutOverlapping(60) in routes/console.php has the same 60-minute expiry.
routes/console.php:13 withoutOverlapping(60) duplicates the command's own Cache::lock. The two use different mutex keys, so this adds ceremony without adding protection.

tests/Feature/PurgeExportsTest.php:36-46 inProduction() doesn't switch to production. It only binds a subclass that always confirms, so the name is misleading, and the comment explains framework internals.
tests/Feature/PurgeExportsTest.php:214-220 dry_run_ignores_the_lock makes no assertion beyond the exit code and never releases the lock if the test fails
strengths: The cutoff is computed once and passed to a #[Scope] olderThan(CarbonInterface) scope, so one builder serves both the dry-run count and the purge
lazyById streams millions of rows with flat memory. Failed rows don't stall the iterator; I probed 2500 rows across chunks with mixed failures. There is an index on created_at.
The file is deleted before the row; a Throwable or a false return from delete() keeps the row, and the error is reported; the run continues and exits with FAILURE
ConfirmableTrait with --force; a refusal returns FAILURE; the dry run needs no confirmation and no lock
Cache::lock in a try/finally plus onOneServer for the two-server schedule

Most thorough test suite: a run larger than one chunk (1200 rows); a mixed false/throw/success disk mock; retry on the next run; the lock being held and then released; invalid --days values (0, -5, abc, 1.5); schedule expression and flags; disk config

v.rationale:
Both commands pass their own tests (impl-2: 20 tests; impl-1: 16 tests). Their command code is nearly identical, and neither has a real bug. Both stream rows with lazyById, delete the file before the row, keep the row when deleting its file fails, report the failure and exit with a failure code. Both use ConfirmableTrait with --force, run the dry run before confirming or locking, guard the purge with Cache::lock in a try/finally, and schedule the nightly run with onOneServer. I added throwaway probe tests to both, then deleted them: 2500 rows across chunks with mixed delete failures, --days=99999999, --force with --no-interaction in production, and a query log. Both behaved identically and kept unbounded queries out.

impl-2 ranks first for two reasons: its scope takes a Carbon cutoff that is computed once, and its tests are clearly stronger. They cover a run larger than one chunk, a disk that throws, more invalid --days values and the disk config. Against it: a 1h lock TTL is risky for millions of rows, the schedule's withoutOverlapping is redundant, and the test helper inProduction() is misnamed. impl-1 is a little leaner and has the safer 6h lock TTL. It also adds the inverse User::exports() relation and names its test helper honestly. But it doesn't test the chunk boundary or a throwing disk, and its scope recomputes now() from an int.
